subject: owl
pitch: A great horned owl perched on a gnarled branch. Mottled bark-brown and buff feathers with fine dark barring, a pale bib at the throat, tall feathered ear tufts, a round tawny facial disc rimmed in black, huge orange eyes and a hooked grey beak. Feathered legs end in strong black talons gripping the wood.
reasoning:
I need to write a single TypeScript module using the SDK that runs reliably without testing, so I'll keep the API calls simple and robust. I'm planning the scale of a great horned owl perched on a gnarled branch resting at ground level, roughly half a meter tall.

Working out the branch geometry as a curved sweep with varying radius so its top sits around y≈0.27, giving the owl's feet a place to grip, then sketching the owl's upright posture with body proportions, hip joint height, and leg length relative to the branch.

I'm figuring out the leg structure as a hip-knee-ankle chain with feathered thigh and short tarsus, planning to build it with explicit joint points rather than a limb helper for more control over foot placement on the branch. Then I'm thinking through the body as a loft of width/height stations from hips to neck base, upright and slightly forward-leaning, while working out the correct options signature for the loft function.

For the head, I'm sketching it as a large sphere-like form with a flattened, scaled sphere for the facial disc, a thin torus for the dark rim around it, and large orange eyes with black pupils positioned relative to the head joint.

Positioning placing both using local "left" offsets so they mirror symmetrically. For the hooked beak, I'm planning a bezier sweep curve projecting forward from the head with a tapering radius to give it that curved raptor shape.

Writing tuft outline...

For the head, I'll use a sphere geometry positioned at the head joint's origin, passing the bone explicitly rather than relying on inference from the position vector.

Now I'm working out the plumage coloring — a mottled bark-brown and buff pattern for the body, considering whether to layer barring stripes with countershading or just use a simple mottle texture with moderate contrast for a naturalistic feathered look.

I'm defining the color palette as hex strings for bark, dark, buff, bib, tawny, rim, eye, beak, talon, branch, and lichen tones, then setting up the spine joint chain running from hips through the back using a curved path with named segments.

I'll skip a separate neck chain and instead parent the head joint directly to the last spine joint, giving it its own position and aim toward the top of the skull. That keeps the hierarchy simple: three spine joints from the named chain, then a head joint attached to spine3.

For the body, I'm lofting through a set of stations along the spine from hips to shoulders, widening in the middle for the rounded owl belly and narrowing near the head, with the countershaded belly color handled through the paint applied afterward. For the wings, I'm thinking of using a sweep or extrude along the sides of the body — a flat drooping feather shape running from the shoulder down the flank, built in the x-y plane with thickness extending outward.

I'll keep thickness consistent on both wing sides since the slab is centered, so the mirroring works fine either way. For feather detail I'll paint barring on the wings, add ear tufts as extruded outlines in the head's XY plane, and build the facial disc as a flattened sphere positioned forward of the head joint, scaled down along the z-axis to keep it shallow.

For the rim around the disc, I'm working out torus placement so it sits on the flattened surface rather than inside or at the hidden equator -- settling on a forward offset of 0.035 with a radius of 0.105 and thin tube so it traces the disc's edge properly. Then I'll place the eyes as small orange spheres offset left/right and forward on the head, with black pupil spheres further forward and a thin eye ring around each.

For the beak I'm sculpting a hooked shape using a bezier sweep between head-local points, tapering the radius so it curves down into a hook, with a small base cover near the head. For the ear tufts I'm extruding a tall pointed outline from a handful of local points to get a tapered tuft shape, then finishing the head itself as a scaled sphere with the facial disc sitting on its front.

Now I'm working out the throat and legs: placing a flattened pale sphere for the bib near the front of the body, then figuring out leg and foot positions so the feet rest on top of a branch. I'm calculating the branch's path and radius so its underside touches the ground while its top surface sits high enough for the feet to perch naturally.

Still shaping the branch path, then adding a couple of small twig sprouts jutting off its surface for extra gnarled detail.

For the bone, I realize the sweep needs an explicit joint rather than defaulting to the nearest one, since that could accidentally link it to something that moves. I'll create a dedicated "perch" joint as a child of the hips root, keep it rigid, and assign the branch sweep to use that bone so it stays fixed in place.

Then I work through the leg chains (hip-knee-ankle joints with a tip joint for the foot), toe placement sinking slightly into the branch for grip, and talon spikes at the tips. I plan the leg sweep radii tapering from thigh to tarsus, and set the tail as a short two-joint chain hanging off the hips, swept with tapering radii.

For the head, I decide to switch from local joint-relative offsets to explicit world coordinates to avoid confusion, and start laying out real-world-scale measurements for a convincing owl size — branch, feet, hips, spine chain, head sphere, flattened facial disc, rim torus, oversized orange eyes with pupils and rims, a curved beak via a four-point bezier, and ear tufts as an extruded outline near the top of the head.

I also plan the wing as an extruded outline hanging along the body, feathered legs, and talons with capsules and spikes for toes gripping the branch, plus a tail chain swept with tapering radii.

For coloring, I set up a layered paint system: a mottled bark-and-buff base with dark stripes layered on top for the feather coat, then apply countershading so the belly reads lighter than the back, and use a separate mottled lichen paint for the branch texture with a couple of gnarly twig sweeps branching off it for realism.

Writing builder code...
